query: Single-phase ZrB2 benefits from strong Zr–B and B–B interactions and a high melting point, but it requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and does not readily meet application requirements on its own. Earlier studies sought to lower the required temperature, yet the resulting materials remained vulnerable to high-temperature oxidation or liquid plating-metal corrosion, while reported preparation temperatures generally remained above 1700 °C. Under the constraints of lower-temperature manufacture, adequate strength and structural integrity, oxidation durability, and prolonged service in a liquid plating bath, what single intervention could overcome these limitations? Provide one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome compared with single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens, applicable preparation and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment evaluating final body quality, structural integrity, oxidation, and liquid-metal corrosion that would falsify the hypothesis if its predictions were not observed.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a minor fraction of hafnium (Hf) into ZrB2 will enable lower‐temperature processing by inducing a transient liquid phase during sintering and, in turn, form in situ Hf‐rich intergranular boundary phases that enhance grain cohesion, oxidation resistance through stable HfO2 formation, and liquid-metal corrosion resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional single-phase ZrB2, which is normally sintered at temperatures >2300 °C and exhibits limited oxidation durability and susceptibility to liquid plating-metal corrosion when processed at lower temperatures.
generation.intervention: Doping ZrB2 with an optimized amount (e.g., approximately 5–10 atomic % Hf) to form a (Zr,Hf)B2 high-entropy solid solution and promote the formation of protective intergranular phases during sintering at reduced temperatures (~1700 °C).
generation.conditions: Fabrication via sintering at approximately 1600–1700 °C with subsequent exposure to high-temperature oxidation conditions and service in a liquid plating-metal bath.
generation.structural_mediator: In situ formed Hf-rich intergranular phases that enhance grain boundary cohesion and act as diffusion barriers, while also facilitating the formation of a stable, passivating HfO2 layer during oxidation.
generation.mechanism: The Hf addition is expected to lower the sintering temperature by promoting a transient liquid-phase sintering mechanism that enhances densification. During service, the Hf-rich phase forms a protective oxide (HfO2) which retards oxygen ingress and minimizes degradation from corrosive liquid metal environments, thereby improving both mechanical integrity and oxidation durability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with high-temperature-sintered conventional single-phase ZrB2 and previously lower-temperature produced specimens, the Hf-doped (Zr,Hf)B2 will exhibit comparable or improved mechanical strength and structural integrity, a lower preparation temperature requirement, and significantly enhanced oxidation and corrosion resistance in liquid metal plating environments.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics of conventional, high-temperature-sintered single-phase ZrB2 and earlier lower-temperature processed variants that suffered from poor oxidation resistance and liquid-metal corrosion.
generation.boundary: The optimized benefits are anticipated when sintering is performed at ~1600–1700 °C and within service temperature ranges typical of high-temperature oxidative and plating-metal corrosive environments; performance outside these temperature windows remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The precise Hf dopant level and processing parameters required to maximize the balance between lower-temperature densification and long-term oxidation/corrosion resistance need further optimization. Moreover, the extent of improvement in liquid-metal corrosion resistance is subject to variability in plating bath composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens: (a) conventional ZrB2 synthesized at >2300 °C (control), and (b) Hf-doped (Zr,Hf)B2 processed at ~1700 °C. Use identical powder precursors and processing conditions except for the Hf addition. Characterize both sets using density measurements, X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase analysis, scanning/transmission electron microscopy (SEM/TEM) for microstructure and grain-boundary phase identification, and mechanical testing (e.g., microhardness and three-point bending). Evaluate oxidation behavior using thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) in an oxygen-rich atmosphere and assess corrosion resistance by immersing samples in a specified liquid plating-metal bath under controlled temperature conditions.
measurements: Relative density (%) and grain size (SEM/TEM analysis)
Phase composition and presence of Hf-rich intergranular phases (XRD, TEM)
Corrosion rate (mass loss measurements after liquid metal exposure)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf-doped specimens processed at lower temperatures do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in densification, mechanical strength, oxidation resistance (lower oxidation weight gain and stable oxide scale formation), and corrosion resistance (reduced mass loss in a liquid metal environment) relative to both the high-temperature-sintered ZrB2 and previously lower-temperature specimens, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Mechanical Alloying as a Way to Produce Metastable Single-Phase High-Entropy Alloys beyond the Stability Criteria

Abstract: Various stability criteria developed for high-entropy alloys are applied to compositions produced by mechanical alloying. While they agree with the annealed samples, these criteria fail to describe the as-milled metastable systems, highlighting the ability of mechanical alloying to overcome the limitations imposed by these criteria. The criteria are based on atomic size (Ω ≥ 1.1 and δr ≤ 6.6%) and/or electronegativity misfit, as well as on mixing enthalpy (Λ>0.95 J mol−1K−1 and −5 kJ mol−1<∆Hmix<0), or purely thermodynamic (ϕYe>20; ϕKing>1; Teff<500 K). These criteria are applied to several compositions found in the literature and to two metastable fcc solid solutions produced by mechanical alloying with compositions Al0.75CoXFeNi with X = Cr and Mn. Single-phase microstructures are stable up to above 600 K, leading to more stable multiphase systems after annealing above this temperature. Study on Microstructure and High Temperature Stability of WTaVTiZrx Refractory High Entropy Alloy Prepared by Laser Cladding

Abstract: The extremely harsh environment of the high temperature plasma imposes strict requirements on the construction materials of the first wall in a fusion reactor. In this work, a refractory alloy system, WTaVTiZrx, with low activation and high entropy, was theoretically designed based on semi-empirical formula and produced using a laser cladding method. The effects of Zr proportions on the metallographic microstructure, phase composition, and alloy chemistry of a high-entropy alloy cladding layer were investigated using a metallographic microscope, XRD (X-ray diffraction), SEM (scanning electron microscope), and EDS (energy dispersive spectrometer), respectively. The high-entropy alloys have a single-phase BCC structure, and the cladding layers exhibit a typical dendritic microstructure feature. The evolution of microstructure and mechanical properties of the high-entropy alloys, with respect to annealing temperature, was studied to reveal the performance stability of the alloy at a high temperature. Rapid liquid phase–assisted ultrahigh-temperature sintering of high-entropy ceramic composites

Abstract: High-entropy ceramics and their composites display high mechanical strength and attractive high-temperature stabilities. However, properties like strong covalent bond character and low self-diffusion coefficients make them difficult to get sintered, limiting their mass popularity. Here, we present a rapid liquid phase–assisted ultrahigh-temperature sintering strategy and use high-entropy metal diboride/boron carbide composite as a proof of concept. We use a carbon-based heater to fast-heat the composite to around 3000 K, and a small fraction of eutectic liquid was formed at the interface between high-entropy metal diborides and boron carbide. A crystalline dodecaboride intergranular phase was generated upon cooling to ameliorate the adhesion between the components. The as-sintered composite presents a high hardness of 36.4 GPa at a load of 0.49 N and 24.4 GPa at a load of 9.8 N. This liquid phase–assisted rapid ultrahigh-temperature strategy can be widely applicable for other ultrahigh-temperature ceramics as well.
